1:1.t: "Blameless": the KJV's "perfect", as in Genesis 6:9. It means whole and sincere, not sinless.

1:3.t: "People of the East": the tribes east of the Jordan, in the region of Edom and Arabia.

1:5.t: "Cursed God": the Hebrew text says "blessed God", a polite substitute used by scribes to avoid writing "curse God". The same is true in 1:11, 2:5 and 2:9.

1:15.t: Sabeans: raiders from Sheba in Arabia.

1:22.t: "Charge God with wrongdoing": the KJV's "charged God foolishly".

3:5.t: "Deep darkness": the KJV's "shadow of death". The Hebrew tsalmavet may mean "deep shadow" or "shadow of death"; see Psalm 23:4.

3:8.t: "Leviathan": the KJV's "their mourning". The Hebrew is livyatan, a sea monster, here pictured as a force of chaos (see 41:1).

3:12.t: "Receive me": the KJV's "prevent me", in the old sense of come before or meet.

3:22.t: "Grave": the Hebrew is qever, the ordinary word for a grave.

4:21.t: "Is not the cord of their tent pulled up": the KJV reads "Doth not their excellency which is in them go away?" The Hebrew yeter can mean "excellence" or "tent cord".

5:1.t: "Holy ones": the KJV's "saints", meaning angels here.

5:5.t: "The thirsty": the KJV's "the robber"; the Hebrew word is uncertain.

5:13.t: Paul quotes this verse in 1 Corinthians 3:19, the only quotation from Job in the New Testament.

6:6.t: "White of an egg": the Hebrew may mean the sap of a plant such as mallow.

6:14.t: The Hebrew of this verse is difficult; the KJV reads "but he forsaketh the fear of the Almighty".

7:6.t: "Hope": the Hebrew tiqvah also means "thread", a wordplay with the weaver's shuttle.

7:12.t: "Monster of the deep": the KJV's "whale"; the Hebrew tannin is a sea monster.

7:20.t: "Have I become a burden to You?": the KJV reads "so that I am a burden to myself". A Jewish scribal tradition says the text was altered from "to You" out of reverence.

8:13.t: "Godless": the KJV's "hypocrite"; the Hebrew chaneph means one who is profane or godless.

9:9.t: "The Bear": the KJV's "Arcturus". The Hebrew constellation names are uncertain. "Constellations of the south": the KJV's "chambers of the south".

9:13.t: "The helpers of Rahab": the KJV's "the proud helpers". Rahab is a mythical sea monster, a picture of chaos (26:12, Psalm 89:10, Isaiah 51:9); it is unrelated to Rahab of Jericho.

9:30.t: "Soap": the KJV's "never so clean"; the Hebrew bor may mean lye or soap.

10:22.t: "Deep darkness": the KJV's "the shadow of death", as at 3:5.

11:6.t: "True wisdom has two sides": the KJV's "that they are double to that which is". The Hebrew is obscure. "God has even forgotten some of your sin": the KJV reads "God exacteth of thee less than thine iniquity deserveth".

11:8.t: "The grave": the KJV's "hell"; Hebrew Sheol. See Genesis 37:35.

11:12.t: The Hebrew is a proverb whose exact sense is debated; the KJV reads "vain man would be wise, though man be born like a wild ass's colt".

12:6.t: "Those who carry their god in their hands": the KJV reads "into whose hand God bringeth abundantly". The Hebrew allows both.

12:19.t: "Priests": the KJV's "princes". The Hebrew word kohanim usually means priests.

13:4.t: "Smear me with lies": the KJV's "forgers of lies", literally "plasterers of lies".

13:27.t: "Putting marks on the soles of my feet": the KJV's "thou settest a print upon the heels of my feet", perhaps like a slave's brand.

14:14.t: "Renewal": the KJV's "change". The Hebrew chaliphah means a change or relief, like a soldier relieved from duty.

"If a man dies, will he live again?": Job's question goes beyond what most of the Old Testament says about life after death. His answer moves from doubt (14:10-12) toward hope (14:13-15), and reaches its height in 19:25-27.

14:16.t: These verses may be read as Job's hope (God will forgive) or as his complaint (God watches every sin). We follow the hopeful reading of verses 13-15.

15:26.t: "Thick, strong shield": the KJV's "the thick bosses of his bucklers".

15:27.t: "His waist bulges with flesh": the KJV's "maketh collops of fat on his flanks".

16:7.t: Job turns from speaking about God to speaking to Him, and then back again, as often in his speeches.

16:13.t: "Kidneys": the KJV's "reins", thought of as the seat of the emotions.

16:15.t: "Brow": the KJV's "horn", a picture of strength and dignity.

17:6.t: "A man in whose face people spit": the KJV reads "aforetime I was as a tabret", taking the Hebrew topheth as a drum. Most read it as "spitting".

17:16.t: "The gates of the grave": the KJV's "the bars of the pit". Hebrew Sheol.

18:13.t: "Death's firstborn": a picture of the deadliest disease.

18:14.t: "The king of terrors": death, pictured as a ruler.

18:20.t: "People of the west ... those of the east": the KJV reads "They that come after him ... as they that went before". The Hebrew can mean either.

19:17.t: "I am loathsome to my own brothers": the KJV reads "though I intreated for the children's sake of mine own body". The Hebrew "sons of my womb" probably means his brothers, sons of his mother's womb, since his own children had died.

19:20.t: "By the skin of my teeth": the source of the English idiom, from the KJV.

19:24.t: "Inscribed with an iron tool on lead": the KJV's "graven with an iron pen and lead", perhaps letters cut in rock and filled with lead.

19:27.t: "How my heart yearns within me": the KJV's "though my reins be consumed within me", literally "my kidneys fail within me", the seat of deep emotion.

20:24.t: "Bronze-tipped arrow": the KJV's "bow of steel"; the Hebrew is "bow of bronze".

21:12.t: "Pipe": the KJV's "organ". The Hebrew ugav was a wind instrument.

21:13.t: "In peace": the KJV's "in a moment". The Hebrew can mean either; the point is a death without suffering.

22:24.t: Ophir: a region famous for fine gold, perhaps in Arabia or East Africa.

22:25.t: "Your gold": the KJV's "thy defence"; the Hebrew betsarekha is the same word as "gold" in verse 24.

22:30.t: "One who is not innocent": the KJV reads "the island of the innocent". The Hebrew i-naqi can mean "not innocent"; the KJV took i as "island".

23:2.t: "His hand": the Hebrew reads "my hand"; the Greek and Syriac read "His hand".

23:8.t: East, west, north, south: the KJV's "forward ... backward ... left ... right". Hebrew orients by facing east.

23:17.t: The Hebrew is difficult; the KJV reads "Because I was not cut off before the darkness".

24:1.t: The KJV reads "Why, seeing times are not hidden from the Almighty, do they that know him not see his days?"

24:18.t: Some scholars think these verses are Job quoting his friends' views; others read them as Job's own belief that the wicked are eventually judged.

25:6.t: "Son of man": here a poetic phrase meaning a human being.

26:5.t: "The spirits of the dead": the KJV's "dead things"; Hebrew repha'im, the shades of the dead.

26:6.t: "The realm of the dead ... Destruction": the KJV's "hell ... destruction"; Hebrew Sheol and Abaddon. Revelation 9:11 uses Abaddon as a name.

26:9.t: "Full moon": the KJV's "his throne". The Hebrew consonants can be read either way.

26:13.t: "The gliding serpent": the KJV's "the crooked serpent", perhaps Leviathan (Isaiah 27:1).

27:1.t: "Discourse": the KJV's "parable"; the Hebrew mashal means a proverb, poem or speech.

27:13.t: Some scholars think these verses belong to a missing third speech of Zophar; in the KJV they are part of Job's speech.

27:23.t: "It claps its hands": the subject may be the east wind (verse 21) or "men", as in the KJV.

28:1.t: The chapter describes ancient mining: shafts sunk into the earth, miners hanging on ropes, rivers dammed to reach ore.

28:22.t: "Destruction and Death": the Hebrew Abaddon and Mavet, pictured as persons.

29:4.t: "Intimate friendship": the KJV's "the secret of God". The Hebrew sod means a circle of close friends or confidential counsel.

30:4.t: "Salt herbs": the KJV's "mallows". "Broom bush": the KJV's "juniper".

30:18.t: The Hebrew of this verse is difficult; the KJV reads "By the great force of my disease is my garment changed".

30:29.t: "Jackals ... owls": the KJV's "dragons ... owls"; the second may be ostriches. Both are creatures of desolate places with mournful cries.

31:1.t: "Not to look lustfully at a young woman": the KJV's "why then should I think upon a maid?" Jesus' teaching on lust in the heart (Matthew 5:28) goes in the same direction.

Job's oath of innocence: in a series of "If I have ... then let ..." statements, Job calls curses on himself if he is guilty. Ancient courts used such oaths when evidence was lacking. With this, Job rests his case and waits for God to answer.

31:10.t: "Grind another man's grain": a picture of servitude and of sexual possession.

31:18.t: The Hebrew is compressed; the KJV reads "he was brought up with me, as with a father, and I have guided her from my mother's womb".

31:27.t: "A kiss of homage": the KJV's "my mouth hath kissed my hand", a gesture of worship toward the sun or moon.

31:31.t: Job means that everyone in his household knew his hospitality; no one went hungry.

31:33.t: "As Adam did": the Hebrew ke'adam can mean "as Adam" (KJV) or "as people do".

31:35.t: "Here is my signature": the Hebrew taw, the last letter of the alphabet, used as a mark or signature.

32:2.t: Elihu: his name means "He is my God". Buz was a son of Nahor, Abraham's brother (Genesis 22:21).

33:6.t: "I am the same as you in God's sight": the KJV reads "I am according to thy wish in God's stead", taking it as Elihu offering to be the arbiter Job asked for (9:33).

33:18.t: "The pit": a term for the grave or the realm of the dead.

33:22.t: "The pit": a term for the grave or the realm of the dead.
"The messengers of death": the KJV's "the destroyers".

33:24.t: "The pit": a term for the grave or the realm of the dead.
"I have found a ransom" (Hebrew kopher): a price paid to release a life. See Exodus 29:33 on kaphar. Jesus says the Son of Man came "to give His life as a ransom for many" (Mark 10:45).

33:28.t: "The pit": a term for the grave or the realm of the dead.

33:30.t: "The pit": a term for the grave or the realm of the dead.

33:26.t: "Restore them to full well-being": the KJV's "render unto man his righteousness".

34:6.t: The KJV reads "Should I lie against my right? my wound is incurable without transgression."

34:29.t: These verses are among the most difficult in Job; the translation follows the general sense.

35:14.t: The Hebrew is difficult; the KJV reads these verses as encouragement to trust God.

36:14.t: "Male prostitutes of the shrines": the KJV's "the unclean". The Hebrew qedeshim; see Deuteronomy 23:17.

36:16.t: These verses are difficult in Hebrew, and translations differ widely.

36:33.t: The Hebrew is obscure; the KJV reads "the cattle also concerning the vapour".

37:22.t: "Golden splendor": the KJV's "fair weather"; the Hebrew zahav means "gold".

37:24.t: The second half may also be read as the KJV does: "he respecteth not any that are wise of heart."

38:3.t: "Brace yourself like a man": the KJV's "Gird up now thy loins like a man", tucking up the robe to be ready for action.

38:17.t: "Deep darkness": the KJV's "the shadow of death"; see 3:5.

38:31.t: "Chains of the Pleiades ... Orion's belt": the KJV's "sweet influences of Pleiades ... bands of Orion".

38:32.t: "The constellations": the KJV's "Mazzaroth", a Hebrew word of uncertain meaning, possibly the signs of the zodiac. "The Bear": the KJV's "Arcturus".

38:36.t: "The ibis ... the rooster": the KJV reads "the inward parts ... the heart". The Hebrew words are rare and may name birds believed to announce the flooding of the Nile and the coming of rain.

38:37.t: "Water jars of the heavens": the KJV's "bottles of heaven", the clouds.

39:13.t: "Stork": the KJV's "ostrich" in the second line; the first line names the ostrich (the KJV's "peacocks"). The Hebrew bird names are uncertain.

39:19.t: "Flowing mane": the KJV's "thunder". The Hebrew ra'mah may mean "quivering" or "mane".

40:15.t: "Behemoth": the plural of the Hebrew behemah, "beast", meaning "the great beast". It may be the hippopotamus, or a symbol of untamable strength.

41:1.t: In the Hebrew Bible, 41:1-8 is 40:25-32, and 41:9-34 is 41:1-26.
"Leviathan": a great sea creature, perhaps the crocodile, and in poetry a symbol of chaos (3:8, Psalm 74:14, Isaiah 27:1).

41:13.t: "Double coat of armor": the KJV's "double bridle".

41:30.t: "Threshing sledge": a heavy board studded with stones, dragged over grain.

42:11.t: "A piece of silver": the Hebrew qesitah, a unit of unknown value; see Genesis 33:19.

42:14.t: Jemimah means "dove"; Keziah means "cassia", a fragrant spice; Keren-happuch means "horn of eye paint". The KJV spells the first two Jemima and Kezia.

1:6.t: "Satan" (Hebrew hassatan, "the adversary" or "the accuser"): in Job the Hebrew has the article, "the satan", describing a role: one who opposes and accuses. The KJV treats it as a name. He appears among the heavenly beings and can act only with God's permission. Later Scripture reveals him more fully as the devil (Revelation 12:9-10).
"The sons of God" (Hebrew bene ha'elohim): heavenly beings, angels, who serve in God's court. See also 38:7.

1:9.t: "Does Job fear God for nothing?" (Hebrew hachinnam): this is the central question of the book: will anyone serve God when it brings no reward? Chinnam means "for free" or "without cause"; God uses the same word in 2:3, "without any reason".

1:21.t: "Naked I came ... the LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away": Job's first response accepts both gifts and losses from God's hand and still blesses Him. Paul echoes the first line in 1 Timothy 6:7.

2:3.t: "Integrity" (Hebrew tummah): wholeness, being consistent through and through. It is related to tam, "blameless" (1:1). Job's wife (2:9) and Job himself (27:5) use the same word.

2:10.t: "Trouble" (Hebrew ra): the word can mean moral evil or simply harm and misfortune. Here it means adversity; the KJV's "evil" does not mean God does wrong.

4:17.t: "Can a mortal be more righteous than God?": the Hebrew can also be read "Can a mortal be righteous before God?" Eliphaz's point, that no human is pure in God's sight, is true in itself; his error is applying it to explain Job's suffering.

5:17.t: "Blessed is the one whom God corrects": compare Proverbs 3:11-12 and Hebrews 12:5-11. Eliphaz speaks a true principle but wrongly assumes Job's suffering is punishment for sin. God later says the friends did not speak rightly (42:7).

6:10.t: "The Holy One" (Hebrew qadosh): a title for God; see Leviticus 11:44-45.

7:17.t: "What is man, that You make so much of him?" (Hebrew mah enosh ki tegaddelennu): Job bitterly parodies Psalm 8:4. The psalmist marvels that God cares for man; Job complains that God watches him too closely.

9:2.t: "How can a mortal be righteous before God?" (Hebrew tsadaq im el): Job uses legal language throughout: to be "righteous" means to be declared in the right, to win one's case. His question is the same one Paul answers in Romans 3-4.

9:33.t: "Someone to arbitrate between us" (Hebrew mokhiach): the KJV's "daysman", an old English word for an arbiter who sets a day for a hearing. Job longs for a mediator who could stand between God and man and lay a hand on both. 1 Timothy 2:5 says there is "one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus." Job's longing grows in 16:19-21 and 19:25.

10:12.t: "Steadfast love" (Hebrew chesed): the KJV's "favour". See Genesis 24:27. Even in his complaint, Job remembers that his life came from God's covenant love.

13:15.t: "Though He slay me, yet I will trust in Him": this is the KJV reading and the reading the Hebrew scribes marked to be read aloud (qere: lo, "in Him"). The written text (ketiv) has lo, "not": "He will slay me; I have no hope." Many modern Bibles follow one or the other. Either way, Job is determined to bring his case before God.

16:19.t: "My witness is in heaven; my advocate is on high" (Hebrew edi ... sahadi): Job, who earlier wished for an arbiter (9:33), now declares that he has a witness in heaven who will speak for him. Sahadi is an Aramaic word meaning the same as edi, "witness". Who this witness is the text does not say; Christians have long heard in it the hope of a heavenly advocate (1 John 2:1).

16:21.t: "He pleads with God": the subject may be the heavenly witness of verse 19, pleading for Job; or the verse may express Job's wish, "Oh that one might plead for a man with God" (KJV).

17:3.t: "Give me the pledge You demand. Who else will put up security for me?": Job asks God Himself to stand as his guarantor, since no one else will. Striking hands was how a guarantee was made (Proverbs 6:1).

19:25.t: "My Redeemer lives" (Hebrew go'ali chai): go'el is the kinsman-redeemer who defends a relative's cause, buys him back, or avenges his blood (see Exodus 6:6, Leviticus 25:25). Job, abandoned by family and friends (19:13-19), declares that he has a living Redeemer who will take his side. Verse 26 shows Job means God Himself, so the word is capitalized. Christians have long heard in this verse a promise fulfilled in Christ, and it is the text of a famous aria in Handel's Messiah.

"In the end ... upon the earth" (Hebrew acharon al aphar): acharon means "last" and can be read "at the last" (as here) or as a title, "the Last One". Aphar means "dust" or "earth", possibly the dust of Job's grave.

19:26.t: "After my skin has been destroyed, yet in my flesh I will see God": the Hebrew mibbesari can mean "from my flesh", that is, in my body, or "apart from my flesh". The KJV and this translation read it as a hope of seeing God in bodily form after death. The verse is one of the Old Testament's strongest expressions of hope beyond the grave.

23:10.t: "When He has tested me, I will come forth as gold": the picture is of refining metal in fire to remove impurities. Job, who cannot find God, still trusts that God knows his way. 1 Peter 1:7 uses the same image of faith tested by fire.

26:7.t: "He suspends the earth over nothing": a striking picture of God's power: the earth rests on nothing but His word.

28:12.t: The poem on wisdom: humans can dig out silver, gold and gems from the depths of the earth, but they cannot dig out wisdom. Only God knows where it is. The poem's answer, in verse 28, is the same as the motto of Proverbs (1:7, 9:10).

28:28.t: "The fear of the Lord, that is wisdom" (Hebrew yir'at adonai hi chokhmah): "the Lord" here is Adonai, not the divine name, as in the KJV. The fear of the Lord is reverent awe and trust that shows itself in turning from evil. This is how Job is described in 1:1, so the poem confirms that Job had true wisdom all along. "Wisdom" (chokhmah): see Exodus 35:31.

29:14.t: "I put on righteousness as my clothing": being clothed with righteousness becomes a common biblical picture (Psalm 132:9, Isaiah 61:10, Ephesians 6:14).

32:8.t: "The spirit in a person, the breath of the Almighty" (Hebrew ruach; nishmat shaddai): see Genesis 1:2 and 2:7. Elihu claims that understanding comes from God's breath, not from age alone.

33:23.t: "An angel ... a mediator" (Hebrew mal'akh melits): mal'akh means a messenger or angel; melits means an interpreter or intercessor. Elihu answers Job's longing for an arbiter (9:33) and witness (16:19): God may send a heavenly mediator to declare a person's uprightness and plead for them.

35:10.t: "Who gives songs in the night": God gives His people songs of praise even in their darkest times. Compare Acts 16:25, where Paul and Silas sing hymns at midnight in prison.

38:1.t: "The LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind": for the first time since chapter 2, the divine name YHWH is used in the narrative. God does not explain Job's suffering or mention the heavenly scene of chapters 1-2. Instead He shows Job the vastness of creation and His own wisdom and care in it.

38:2.t: "Who is this that darkens My counsel": counsel (etsah) means God's plan or purpose for the world. Job's words, though honest, spoke of things he did not understand (42:3).

38:7.t: "The sons of God": angels; see 1:6. They rejoiced at the creation of the world.

38:41.t: "When its young cry out to God": God's care reaches even the raven. Jesus says, "Consider the ravens ... God feeds them" (Luke 12:24).

40:4.t: "I am unworthy" (Hebrew qalloti, "I am light, insignificant"): the opposite of kavod, "weight, glory". Before God's glory, Job recognizes how small he is.

41:10.t: "Who then is able to stand against Me? Who has a claim against Me that I must pay?": the point of the speeches about Behemoth and Leviathan: if Job cannot master these creatures, he cannot sit in judgment on their Maker. Paul quotes verse 11 in Romans 11:35.

42:5.t: "My ears had heard of You, but now my eyes have seen You": Job's suffering is not explained, but he has met God, and that encounter answers his deepest need.

42:6.t: "I despise myself and repent in dust and ashes" (Hebrew em'as venichamti al aphar va'epher): the verb ma'as has no object in Hebrew; it may mean "I reject" my words or "I melt away". Nicham (see Genesis 6:6) can mean "repent", "relent", or "be comforted". Many read it as Job withdrawing his complaint before God; some read "I am comforted, though I am dust and ashes".

42:7.t: "You have not spoken the truth about Me, as My servant Job has" (Hebrew nekhonah, "what is right, firm"): God vindicates Job and rebukes the friends, who defended God with false claims that suffering always means sin. Job's honest wrestling was closer to the truth. James 5:11 commends "the endurance of Job".

42:10.t: "Restored his fortunes" (Hebrew shav et shevut): the KJV's "turned the captivity". See Deuteronomy 30:3.
